Yes. 

The manipulation of time in the story is very effective and well-balanced. Because the piece is written in a dramatic script format, the "story time" of the immediate scene closely matches the "real-world time" it takes to read it, allowing the awkwardness and tension between Martin and Jörg to play out naturally. 

At the same time, the writer uses extreme **compression of time** through subtext and dialogue to summarize years of estrangement and major life events—the dissolution of their shared business (indicated by the weathered and replaced sign), unanswered letters, and the illness and death of Jörg’s father—into just a few brief, loaded lines. Conversely, **stretching of time** is used subtly through stage directions (*"Pause"*, *"Lange Stille"*, *"Er sieht lange auf seine Tasse"*) and the drawn-out interaction over the sugar bowl, which slows the pacing down at crucial emotional turning points to emphasize what remains unsaid between the two men.
